title: The jar of perfume (John 12:1–8)
hookLine: Mary of Bethany pours a year's wages of perfume on his feet

cards: Flowers that cost too much. A friend who drives all night to be there. A gift so over the top that nobody at the party knows where to look.
Back in Bethany, six days before Passover, John says, they make Jesus a supper. Lazarus, called out of the tomb, is at the table. His sister Martha is serving.
And their sister Mary brings out a pound of very costly ointment.

teach.b: John tells it, in the King James Bible: "Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment."
Spikenard, or nard, was a precious perfumed oil. She doesn't dab it.

teach.h: SHE WIPED HIS FEET WITH HER HAIR.
teach.b: She pours a whole pound on his feet, wipes them with her own hair in front of everyone, and the whole house smells of it.
Then Judas speaks, and on paper he has a point: "Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?"
Three hundred pence is three hundred denarii, and in Matthew's parable of the vineyard a laborer is paid a penny a day. So this is three hundred days of work.
John adds, bluntly, that Judas kept the common purse and helped himself from it.

teach.h: AGAINST THE DAY OF MY BURYING.
teach.b: Jesus answers: "Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this."

teach.h: THE HOUSE WAS FILLED WITH THE ODOUR.
teach.b: Later in John, his body is wrapped with spices for the grave. Mary, it seems, understood something the others didn't: he was about to die. Then: "For the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always."

That line has been misused to excuse ignoring the poor. But it echoes Deuteronomy, where the same thought comes with a command: open your hand wide to the poor. One way to hear it: the choice isn't generosity or love.

how: Many churches read the anointing at Bethany in Holy Week, and in Catholic and Orthodox churches, anointing with oil and perfume remains part of baptism, confirmation or chrismation, and prayer for the sick. Mary of Bethany is remembered with her sister Martha and brother Lazarus.

o: a cheap oil burned in lamps in every home
a costly perfumed oil, poured out on his feet
a bitter herb eaten at the Passover meal

games.q: who said or did what — tap the pairs.
p: why not sold for three hundred pence?

s: Judas valued the ointment at three hundred pence
three hundred denarii. in Matthew's vineyard parable, a laborer earns one a day.
Jesus said the poor didn't matter
his words echo Deuteronomy, which comes with a command to open your hand to the poor.
the Mary in this story is Lazarus's sister
Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha and Lazarus.

games.q: you're at the table in Bethany. Mary has just poured a pound of very costly ointment on Jesus's feet. Judas says it should have been sold for the poor. what does Jesus say?
o: Judas is right. she should have sold it.
let her alone. she kept it for my burial.
games.why: let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this. Mary seems to understand what's coming.

practice: Think of someone who deserves more praise than they get: a parent, a teacher, a friend, a coworker who quietly holds things together.
Compose one extravagant compliment for them, not a polite one but too much, the kind that fills the room, saying exactly what they mean to you and why.
Notice if it feels embarrassing; Mary's gift drew an objection at the table, and she gave it anyway. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.

wordCard.voice: Spikenard. The costly perfumed oil Mary poured, a whole pound of it, on Jesus's feet, and wiped with her own hair. This week's words: the keys, transfiguration, Zacchaeus up a sycamore, Lazarus, hosanna, the moneychangers' tables go over. And now three hundred pence poured out.

orig.note: Greek: nard, spikenard, a costly perfumed oil, the ointment Mary pours out.

carryVoice: Your line: love can be lavish. Tomorrow, a basin and a towel. Week nine, complete.
